key_insight: Adversarial edits exposed missed anatomy, diagnostic certainty, and severity details in LLM-generated patient-friendly radiology summaries, even in the highest-scoring model.
clinical_relevance: These errors could change patients’ understanding of radiology findings, underscoring the need to verify that summaries preserve clinically meaningful details.
method: Applied controlled term substitutions and impression removals to CT and MRI reports using a radiologist-validated dictionary.
Tested six LLMs with two prompt styles across 18,000 evaluation pairs.
Used an LLM judge to score faithfulness, edit sensitivity, certainty fidelity, and hallucinations.
evidence_signal: GPT-5-mini scored highest for faithfulness and certainty fidelity but had 28.1–30.1% hallucination rates under term substitution; judge–radiologist agreement on 105 cases was macro-F1 0.55–0.56.
watch_item: Automated scoring had only moderate agreement with radiologists, and this evaluation does not establish safety in real-world patient use.
paper_title: Adversarial Evaluation of Large Language Models for Patient-Friendly Radiology Report Summarization
